content: Inhaled beta2-agonist therapy is a cornerstone in the management of acute asthma. However, in severe cases, the delivery of inhaled medication to the small conducting airways may be compromised. In such situations, intravenous (IV) administration of bronchodilators may provide a faster therapeutic response. Both IV beta2-agonists and IV aminophylline are potential options for additional treatment in these scenarios. This review aims to compare the efficacy and safety of IV beta2-agonists versus IV aminophylline in the treatment of acute asthma, particularly in emergency department settings and hospitalized patients with severe asthma. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified through a systematic search of the Cochrane Airways Group Register, which includes data from bibliographic databases, respiratory journals, and conference abstracts. The most recent search was conducted in September 2012. Additional studies were identified by reviewing bibliographies of included studies and consulting primary authors and content experts. The inclusion criteria focused on RCTs involving patients with acute asthma treated with either IV beta2-agonists or IV aminophylline. Two independent reviewers assessed the methodological quality of the studies and extracted data for analysis. A total of 11 studies met the inclusion criteria, encompassing 350 patients. However, the ability to combine these studies in meta-analyses was limited due to variability in the reported outcomes. Length of Stay: Two pediatric studies, including one conducted in a pediatric intensive care unit, reported on the length of hospital stay. No significant difference was observed between the IV beta2-agonist and IV aminophylline groups (mean difference [MD] 23.19 hours; 95% confidence interval [CI] -2.40 to 48.77 hours; 2 studies; N = 73). Separate analyses of the two studies also showed no significant difference. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the small number of trials and participants. Pulmonary Function: No significant differences in pulmonary function, whether sequential or cumulative, were observed between the two treatment groups across the included studies. Heart Rate: Three studies reported serial heart rate data at various time points ranging from 15 to 60 minutes. No significant differences were found between the IV beta2-agonist and IV aminophylline groups. However, a single small study reported a statistically significant difference in final heart rate favoring the beta2-agonist group (MD 10.00; 95% CI 0.99 to 19.01). This result should be interpreted with caution due to the limited sample size. Adverse Effects: Analyses of adverse effects showed that beta2-agonists were associated with significantly fewer side effects compared to aminophylline. Specifically, beta2-agonists were favored in terms of lower rates of giddiness (odds ratio [OR] 59.22; 95% CI 2.80 to 1253.05; 1 study; N = 30), combined nausea/vomiting (OR 14.18; 95% CI 1.62 to 124.52; 2 studies; N = 96), and nausea alone (OR 6.53; 95% CI 1.60 to 26.72; 2 studies; N = 49). However, these findings are based on a very small number of studies and participants, necessitating cautious interpretation. A related review also suggests a higher incidence of adverse effects with IV aminophylline when used in combination with beta2-agonists. Conclusions: The included RCTs did not provide consistent evidence favoring either IV beta2-agonists or IV aminophylline for the treatment of acute asthma. The ability to draw definitive conclusions is limited by the heterogeneity of outcomes assessed and the small sample sizes of the included studies. These findings should be considered alongside evidence from other Cochrane reviews that compare IV beta2-agonists plus inhaled beta2-agonists versus inhaled beta2-agonists alone, as well as IV aminophylline plus inhaled beta2-agonists versus inhaled beta2-agonists alone.
